The expected change over a day is the total derivative, which includes the drift term: dc = theta*dt + delta*E[dS] + (1/2)*gamma*E[dS^2]. The theta term is negative, but delta*mu*S*dt is positive and larger, and the gamma term is positive too. So the expectation is positive while the partial is negative. The everyday version: a long option position loses money on most days and makes a lot on a few, and the average is positive. Negative theta and positive expected return describe different slices of the same distribution.
questions.technique: Partial versus total derivative; real-world versus risk-neutral drift
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: it sounds paradoxical, and the resolution requires being precise about what is held fixed.

questions.prompt: You sell a one-week at-the-money straddle and delta-hedge it daily. What are you short?
options: Gamma and vega - and long theta
Delta and gamma
Theta and vega
Nothing - the delta hedge makes you flat
questions.explanation: Short gamma and short vega, long theta. Delta-hedging removes your first-order spot exposure, which is exactly what makes the remaining exposures the point of the trade rather than a side effect. Short gamma means the daily rebalancing forces you to buy after rises and sell after falls - you lose on realised movement. Short vega means a rise in implied vol marks you down immediately. Long theta is the compensation: you collect time decay every day the stock sits still. The position is a bet that realised volatility over the week comes in below the implied vol you sold, and being short-dated and at-the-money maximises both the gamma and the theta, so it is the most concentrated version of that bet available.
questions.technique: Greek exposures of a delta-hedged short straddle
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the sign of each Greek must be right, and 'flat' is a real temptation after delta hedging.

questions.prompt: Which option has the most vega?
options: A long-dated at-the-money option
A short-dated at-the-money option
A long-dated deep in-the-money option
A short-dated deep out-of-the-money option
questions.explanation: Long-dated and at-the-money. Vega is S*phi(d1)*sqrt(T), so it scales with sqrt(T) - the opposite of gamma, which blows up as T goes to zero. It is also maximised near the money, where phi(d1) peaks. The intuition is that volatility is a rate per unit of root-time, so it has more time to act on a long-dated option, while a deep in- or out-of-the-money option's fate is largely settled and extra vol barely changes it. This opposite maturity dependence is why desks separate the two risks: you trade short-dated options for gamma and long-dated ones for vega, and a book can easily be long gamma and short vega at the same time.
questions.technique: Vega's maturity and moneyness profile
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: easy to confuse with gamma, which has the opposite maturity dependence.

questions.prompt: You are delta-hedged and long a one-month at-the-money option. Write down, approximately, your profit and loss over a single day, and say what determines whether it is positive.
questions.canonicalAnswer: P&L is approximately (1/2)*gamma*S^2*[(dS/S)^2 - sigma^2*dt]. It is positive when the day's realised move is bigger than the implied move you paid for.
questions.explanation: Take a Taylor expansion of the option value in time and spot. The delta term is hedged away, leaving dP&L = theta*dt + (1/2)*gamma*(dS)^2. Substituting the PDE relation theta = -(1/2)*sigma^2*S^2*gamma (exact when r = 0) gives dP&L = (1/2)*gamma*S^2*[(dS/S)^2 - sigma^2*dt]. Read it directly: gamma is the size of the bet, and what you are betting on is whether the squared realised return beats the squared implied return over the day. Being long an option and delta-hedged is a long realised-vol, short implied-vol position, day by day. Consequences worth stating. The break-even daily move is sigma*sqrt(dt) - for a 16% vol that is about 1% a day, which is the origin of the desk shorthand 'vol over sixteen is your daily move'. The P&L depends on the SQUARE of the move, so direction is irrelevant and a few large days dominate the total. And gamma is a weight, so the same vol view expressed in short-dated at-the-money options is far more levered than in long-dated ones.
questions.technique: Gamma P&L: realised versus implied volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the formula is standard, but reading it as a vol bet is the substance.

questions.prompt: A call and a put on the same non-dividend-paying stock, both struck at $100 with one year left, trade at $8 and $5. The stock is at $100 and the interest rate is zero. Is there an arbitrage, and what exactly do you trade?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Yes. Parity requires C - P = S - K*e^(-rT) = 0, so the call is $3 too rich relative to the put. Sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock, and borrow $100. You collect $3 today for a position that is worth exactly zero at expiry.
questions.explanation: Check parity: C - P should equal S - K*e^(-rT) = 100 - 100 = 0, so the call and put should trade at the same price. They differ by $3, so the call is rich (or the put is cheap - parity cannot tell you which, only that the combination is mispriced). Trade the combination that is overpriced. The synthetic short stock, being short a call and long a put, pays -max(S-100,0) + max(100-S,0) = 100 - S at expiry. So: sell the call (+$8), buy the put (-$5), buy the stock (-$100), borrow $100 (+$100). Net cash today: +$3. At expiry the stock is worth S, the option combination is worth 100 - S, and you repay the $100 loan - total exactly zero, whatever the stock does. You have collected $3 for a portfolio with no residual exposure. Before declaring victory in an interview, name the reasons this usually is not free money: the options may be American, in which case early assignment on the short call breaks the static hedge; borrow cost or hard-to-borrow status on the stock; an unexpected dividend, which would break the no-dividend assumption; and whether $3 survives the bid-offer on three legs. If none of those bite, it is a genuine arbitrage.
questions.technique: Trading the put-call parity violation
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: spotting it is easy; getting all four legs and their signs right is where people slip.

questions.prompt: You are delta-hedged and short gamma. What kind of market do you want?
options: A quiet, range-bound one
A trending one
A volatile one
It makes no difference once you are delta-hedged
questions.explanation: Quiet. Short gamma means your daily P&L is roughly -(1/2)*gamma*S^2*[(realised move)^2 - (implied move)^2], so you profit only when realised movement comes in below what you sold. Every large move costs you, in either direction, because the P&L depends on the square. A trending market is bad for a different reason worth naming: the delta hedge forces you to buy after every rise and sell after every fall, so a persistent trend grinds you down through the rebalancing itself. The one thing you own is theta, and theta only pays if nothing happens.
questions.technique: P&L profile of a short-gamma position
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: direct application of the gamma P&L identity.

questions.prompt: Your desk reports a one-day 99% VaR of $1 million. What does that mean?
options: The worst you can lose in a day is $1 million
On about 1% of days you should expect to lose more than $1 million
You expect to lose $1 million on average across the worst 1% of days
You will lose $1 million once every hundred days, on average, and never more
questions.explanation: VaR is a THRESHOLD on the loss distribution, not a bound and not an average. A one-day 99% VaR of $1m says that on roughly one day in a hundred, losses should exceed $1m - and it says nothing whatever about how much worse than $1m they might be. That silence about the tail is VaR's central weakness, and it is exactly what Expected Shortfall fixes: the third answer is the definition of ES, which will always be larger than the corresponding VaR. The first answer is the classic misreading that gets people into trouble, since a distribution with a fat tail can have a modest VaR and catastrophic losses beyond it.
questions.technique: Reading a VaR number correctly
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: definitional, but the 'worst case' misreading is remarkably persistent.

questions.prompt: Which VaR methodology makes no assumption about the shape of the return distribution?
options: Historical simulation
Parametric (variance-covariance)
Monte Carlo
All three are distribution-free
questions.explanation: Historical simulation. It simply replays actual past return vectors through today's portfolio and reads the relevant percentile off the resulting empirical distribution, so fat tails and skew are captured to whatever extent they occurred in the sample window. Parametric VaR assumes normality (or another named distribution) and reduces to a z-score times the portfolio standard deviation - fast, analytic, and systematically too thin in the tails. Monte Carlo does not assume normal RETURNS but does assume a model you specify to generate them, so it trades one assumption for another - flexible, but only as good as the model. Historical simulation's own weakness is that it is entirely backward-looking: if the window contains no crash, the model does not believe in crashes, and its effective sample size in the far tail is tiny.
questions.technique: Comparing the three VaR methodologies
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: a straight comparison, though the Monte Carlo distinction needs care.

questions.prompt: A $100 million portfolio has a daily volatility of 1%. Assuming zero mean and normal returns, what is its one-day 99% parametric VaR?
options: $1.00 million
$1.65 million
$2.33 million
$2.58 million
questions.explanation: $2.33 million. Parametric VaR is z * sigma * V, and the 99% one-tailed normal critical value is 2.326. So 2.326 * 0.01 * 100m = $2.33m. The distractors are the numbers you must not confuse: 1.645 is the 95% one-tailed value, and 2.576 is the 99% TWO-tailed value - wrong here, because VaR only cares about the loss tail. The three you should have memorised are 1.645 for 95%, 2.326 for 99%, and 1.282 for 90%. Worth adding that this figure is almost certainly too low in practice: real daily equity returns are fat-tailed, so the true 1% quantile sits further out than the normal assumption implies.
questions.technique: Parametric VaR and one-tailed normal quantiles
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: one multiplication, but only if you pick the right critical value.

questions.prompt: How do you scale a one-day VaR to a ten-day VaR, assuming returns are independent and identically distributed?
options: Multiply by sqrt(10), about 3.16
Multiply by 10
Multiply by 10/sqrt(2)
You cannot - VaR does not scale
questions.explanation: Multiply by sqrt(10) = 3.16. Under iid returns, variances add across days, so standard deviations - and hence any fixed quantile of a distribution that keeps its shape - scale with the square root of the horizon. This is the square-root-of-time rule that Basel permitted for scaling one-day VaR to the ten-day regulatory horizon. Its assumptions fail in exactly the situations you care about: volatility clusters (so a bad day predicts more bad days, and the true multiple exceeds sqrt(10)), returns are autocorrelated in stressed or illiquid markets, and portfolio composition changes within the window. The rule also requires the distributional shape to be stable across horizons, which aggregation slowly undermines.
questions.technique: Square-root-of-time scaling and where it breaks
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the rule is standard; knowing its failure modes is the differentiator.

questions.prompt: Why is Expected Shortfall preferred to VaR under the FRTB rules? What property does VaR lack?
questions.canonicalAnswer: VaR is not subadditive, so it is not a coherent risk measure - it can report that a diversified portfolio is riskier than the sum of its parts. ES is subadditive, and it also describes the size of losses beyond the threshold rather than ignoring them.
questions.explanation: Two distinct reasons. First, coherence. A risk measure should satisfy subadditivity: risk(A + B) <= risk(A) + risk(B), so that combining positions never increases measured risk. VaR fails this in general, which has awkward consequences - it can penalise diversification, and it means desk-level VaRs cannot be safely aggregated or used for limit-setting without the whole thing being gameable. ES is subadditive and, together with the other axioms, coherent. Second, tail blindness. VaR is a quantile, so it is completely insensitive to the shape of the distribution beyond it. A book can shorten its tail or lengthen it enormously with no change in VaR at all. That makes VaR manipulable in a specific way: sell deep out-of-the-money options, collect the premium, and the losses land beyond the threshold where VaR cannot see them - your measured risk falls while your actual risk rises. ES averages the losses beyond the threshold, so it responds to exactly that trade. FRTB moved to a 97.5% ES, chosen so that for a normal distribution it corresponds roughly to a 99% VaR, keeping the calibration familiar while fixing the properties. The honest counterpoint, worth raising: ES is harder to backtest, because it is a conditional expectation over rare events rather than a simple exception count, and that was the main argument for keeping VaR.
questions.technique: Coherence and subadditivity of risk measures
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: naming subadditivity is the core; the tail-blindness argument makes it complete.

questions.prompt: Give a concrete example in which VaR is not subadditive.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Two independent bonds, each defaulting with probability 4% and losing $100. At 95% confidence each has VaR of 0, but the portfolio has a 7.84% chance of at least one default, so its 95% VaR is $100 - which exceeds the sum of the individual VaRs.
questions.explanation: Take two bonds, independent, each defaulting with probability 4% and losing $100 if it does, otherwise nothing. Individually: the loss exceeds 0 only 4% of the time, and 4% < 5%, so the 95% quantile of each loss distribution is 0. VaR(A) = VaR(B) = 0. Together, holding one of each: P(no default) = 0.96^2 = 0.9216, so P(at least one default) = 7.84% > 5%. The 95% quantile of the portfolio loss therefore sits at $100. So VaR(A + B) = 100 > 0 = VaR(A) + VaR(B). Subadditivity is violated by the maximum possible amount. What went wrong is not the independence - it is that VaR is a quantile of a discontinuous distribution, and combining positions can push probability mass across the threshold. Note that Expected Shortfall behaves correctly here: ES at 95% for each bond alone is 0.04/0.05 * 100 = $80, so the sum is $160, while the portfolio ES is lower. Two lessons for practice: VaR limits set desk by desk can be violated by the aggregate even when every desk complies, and VaR misbehaves worst for portfolios with lumpy, discontinuous payoffs - credit, and short-option books.

questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the construction needs default probabilities straddling the confidence level, which is a specific trick.

questions.prompt: You backtest a 99% one-day VaR model over 250 trading days and observe 9 exceptions. Are you concerned, and what do you do next?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Yes, seriously. You expect 2.5 exceptions; 9 is far into the tail and a Kupiec test rejects the model. Under Basel's traffic-light system 10 or more is the red zone and 9 is deep in yellow, meaning a capital multiplier. Then check whether the exceptions were clustered.
questions.explanation: Start with the expected count: 250 * 0.01 = 2.5. Observing 9 is more than triple that. Under the null the count is Binomial(250, 0.01), whose standard deviation is sqrt(250*0.01*0.99) = 1.57, so 9 is over four standard deviations out - the Kupiec proportion-of-failures test rejects comfortably. Basel's traffic light puts 5-9 exceptions in the yellow zone, escalating the capital multiplier, with 10 or more triggering red. So 9 is the worst yellow reading there is. The next step is Christoffersen's independence test. Nine exceptions scattered evenly across the year and nine exceptions falling in a single fortnight are very different diagnoses. Scattered suggests the model is simply calibrated too tight - the volatility estimate is too low, or the tails are too thin because of a normality assumption. Clustered suggests the model fails to respond to changing volatility, which is what a static covariance window does when vol clusters: it is fine in calm regimes and hopelessly late in stressed ones. The fix follows the diagnosis: fat-tailed or historical-simulation quantiles for the first, an EWMA or GARCH volatility estimate for the second. And check the mundane possibilities before rewriting the model - a mismapped position, a stale price series, or a new product not captured by the risk factors will produce exactly this signature.
questions.technique: Backtesting VaR: unconditional coverage and independence
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the count test is straightforward; knowing to test clustering separately is what shows depth.

questions.prompt: The Kupiec test checks whether the number of VaR exceptions is consistent with the stated confidence level. What does the Christoffersen test add?
options: It checks whether exceptions are independent over time rather than clustered
It checks whether the exceptions are large enough
It corrects for the finite sample size
It tests whether the portfolio's composition changed during the window
questions.explanation: Christoffersen tests INDEPENDENCE - whether an exception today predicts an exception tomorrow. Kupiec only counts exceptions, so it is a test of unconditional coverage and cannot distinguish 5 exceptions spread across the year from 5 in one week. But those mean different things: clustering says the model is not tracking a changing volatility regime, which is the more dangerous failure, because it means the model is most wrong precisely when the losses arrive. Christoffersen's combined test of conditional coverage nests both, checking the rate and the independence together. Neither test looks at the SIZE of the exceptions, which is the structural reason ES is hard to backtest - you would need the magnitudes, not just the indicator.
questions.technique: Unconditional coverage versus conditional coverage
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the distinction between count and clustering is the whole content.

questions.prompt: Why does parametric VaR tend to understate risk badly in a crisis?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Four reasons compounding: real returns are fat-tailed so the normal quantile is too close in; correlations move toward 1 in stress so measured diversification evaporates; a trailing covariance estimate is stale when volatility clusters; and the assumed liquidation horizon becomes unachievable.
questions.explanation: The failures compound rather than adding. (1) Fat tails. Parametric VaR multiplies a volatility estimate by a normal quantile. Real daily returns have far more extreme observations than a normal - moves that should occur once in a century show up every few years - so the 99% point is further out than 2.33 standard deviations. (2) Correlation breakdown. The covariance matrix is estimated in normal conditions, where diversification looks real. In a crisis correlations converge toward 1 as everything sells off together, so the diversification benefit embedded in the matrix disappears at exactly the moment it was supposed to protect you. Portfolio vol is therefore understated by the most when it matters most. (3) Stale volatility. Volatility clusters, so an equally-weighted trailing window understates risk entering a stressed period and overstates it leaving one. An EWMA or GARCH estimate reacts faster but still lags a genuine regime break. (4) Liquidity and horizon. VaR assumes you can exit within the stated horizon at marked prices. In stress, spreads widen, size disappears, and the one-day assumption becomes fiction - so the loss you actually take exceeds the loss the distribution described even if the distribution was right. On top of these, the whole framework is estimated on historical data, so it cannot price a risk it has never observed. This is why VaR is supplemented rather than trusted: stressed VaR calibrated to a crisis window, explicit scenario analysis, and stress tests that impose correlations rather than estimating them.
questions.technique: Failure modes of the variance-covariance approach
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: several partial answers exist; naming correlation breakdown and liquidity is what makes it strong.

questions.prompt: A trader systematically sells deep out-of-the-money options and the desk's reported VaR falls. What has happened?
options: VaR is blind to what happens beyond its threshold, so premium income is visible while the tail loss is not
The options genuinely reduce portfolio risk through diversification
The VaR model is broken and should be recalibrated
Nothing unusual - selling options always reduces VaR
questions.explanation: This is the textbook way to game a VaR limit. Selling deep out-of-the-money options brings in premium every day and produces losses only in scenarios rarer than the VaR confidence level - so those losses land beyond the quantile, where VaR literally cannot see them. Measured risk falls, P&L looks steady and impressive, and the actual exposure is a large short tail. The strategy is sometimes described as picking up nickels in front of a steamroller, and the pattern - smooth returns punctuated by a catastrophic quarter - recurs through the history of blowups. The model is not broken; it is doing exactly what a quantile does, which is why the fix is a different measure. Expected Shortfall averages losses beyond the threshold and therefore charges for precisely this trade, which is one of the main reasons FRTB switched to it. Stress testing and explicit tail-scenario limits do the same job from another direction.
questions.technique: How a quantile-based limit can be gamed
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: requires connecting the payoff shape to the measure's blind spot.
